My first period is
irregular: is that normal?
Yes, that’s completely normal. Here’s why the cycle takes time to settle down, and when it’s worth talking about it.
Why the cycle is irregular at first
How long it takes to settle down
The hormones that regulate the cycle take time to find their balance. It’s therefore common for cycles to be shorter, longer, or spaced unevenly during the first few years.
The cycle can take one to two years, sometimes a bit more, to become more regular. This adjustment period varies a lot from person to person, without it being a problem.
An irregular cycle at first is never considered a delay: your body is simply taking the time it needs.

In the vast majority of cases, there’s nothing to worry about. That said, it’s a good idea to see a doctor if your period is absent for several months after it first appears, or if you have ongoing doubts.
No period for several months, very intense pain, or very heavy bleeding.

Which protection should I choose
for my first period?
There are several ways to protect yourself during your period. None is better than another — personal comfort is what guides the choice.
How to choose based on your comfort

For your first period, a pad is usually the simplest protection to use, since it goes directly into your underwear. Period underwear and tampons are other options you can try later, whenever you feel like it.
Easy to use, they go in your underwear and are changed regularly.
Absorbent, washable underwear that’s comfortable for everyday use.
Inserted inside the body; whether and when to use them is up to you, at your own pace.

There’s no right or wrong protection: each one suits different bodies, habits, and comfort levels. Tampons, for example, are inserted inside the body and call for a bit more familiarity with it — nothing says you have to use them from your very first period.
Trying different types of protection over time helps you find the one that suits you best, with no pressure.
On average, protection should be changed every 4 to 6 hours, more often on heavier-flow days. Changing it regularly helps you stay comfortable and keep up good intimate hygiene.

Early signs
of your first period
Your body often gives hints before your very first period arrives. Recognizing them can help you feel less surprised.

In the months before your first period, your body changes gently: your shape evolves, body hair starts appearing in new places, and sweating changes too. These are normal effects of puberty, gently preparing your body.
These changes don’t all happen at the same time, or at the same pace, for everyone — that’s completely normal.
Your body changes gradually: your shape, body hair, and sweating can all shift.
Light, whitish discharge often appears a few months before your first period.
You may feel slight tension or twinges in your lower belly.
It’s common to feel more sensitive or irritable than usual.
You may notice slight tenderness or swelling.
These signs usually mean your first period will arrive in the following months, though it’s impossible to predict an exact date. Keeping protection close at hand becomes a good habit at this point.
These signs are general guides, never a precise prediction. Every body follows its own pace.

Period flow: understanding
colors and textures
The color and texture of your period say a lot about your hormonal health. Learn to read them to better understand your cycle.
Our tips to help you know yourself better
Fresh flow, new blood. Common at the start of your period.
Older blood, normal in the middle of the cycle.
Oxidized blood, often at the end of your period.
May indicate light flow or a hormonal change.
May be linked to an infection or an imbalance.
Pieces of tissue or mucous membrane.
Normal cycle. Your body is shedding the uterine lining.
Older blood, nothing to worry about.
May occur at the start/end of your period or with a hormonal imbalance.
Keep an eye on it if accompanied by a strong odor, itching, or pain.
Very heavy bleeding (changing protection every 1–2 hours)
Based on your flow and your comfort.

Taking care of your intimate hygiene
during your period
Caring for your intimate hygiene means respecting your body and its natural balance.
During your period, your body changes and becomes more sensitive. Adopting the right habits helps prevent irritation and infection, and helps you stay comfortable day to day.
Wash gently: a simple rinse with clear water, from front to back, is enough to protect your natural flora.
Change your protection regularly: every 4 to 6 hours to avoid moisture and unpleasant odors.
Choose cotton: cotton underwear lets your skin breathe and reduces the risk of irritation.
Vaginal douches, which disrupt your natural flora
Keeping a damp pad or tampon on for too long
Unusual odor or discharge that’s different from what’s normal for you
Significant pain or symptoms that worry you
Your body already has a natural balancing mechanism. A gentle wash is usually enough.

Pill, patch, ring, implant, hormonal IUD: what sets them apart and how to think about the method that best fits your daily life.
Hormonal methods use hormones to prevent pregnancy. Depending on the method, they can mainly prevent ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, and change the uterine environment.
Several mechanisms may contribute to protection.
Some methods prevent or inhibit the release of the egg.
The mucus may become thicker, which makes it harder for sperm to get through.
The combination of these mechanisms helps reduce the risk of pregnancy.
Not all methods call for the same level of involvement. The main difference is how often you need to think about your contraception.
From a daily action to long-term protection
Ideal if you want to manage your own contraception
Convenient if you’d rather avoid a daily routine
A discreet option with few day-to-day actions
Suited if you want long-term contraception
A long-term solution that needs very little upkeep
The fewer day-to-day actions a method requires, the less often you need to think about it. This can be worth considering if you know you’re likely to forget a dose or a change.
There isn’t one ideal method for everyone. The best choice depends on your daily life, your preferences, your tolerance, and your plans.
Some methods call for a daily action, while others work for several weeks or years.
How a method feels can vary from person to person. Talking with a healthcare professional can help you work out what suits you.
If you’re hoping for a pregnancy soon or later on, the method’s duration and reversibility can help guide your choice.
Discretion, simplicity, no daily routine, or long-lasting protection: your priorities matter in this decision.
A quick question to help you decide
“Would I rather think about my contraception every day, every week, or only a few times a year?”
Pill or a method that needs regular attention
Patch or ring, depending on the rhythm you choose

Choosing a hormonal contraceptive should take your personal and medical situation into account. A healthcare professional can help you compare the benefits, risks, contraindications, and possible side effects.
The key points to keep in mind
Hormonal methods use different hormone combinations and different schedules of use.
The pill, patch, and ring call for ongoing involvement, while the implant and hormonal IUD are long-term methods.
The choice should fit your daily life, your preferences, your tolerance, and your plans.
No method is universally “best” — it mainly needs to be compatible with your needs and your situation.
Taking the time to compare methods with a healthcare professional helps you choose a contraception you can use calmly and consistently.

Why they happen, how to identify your triggers, and what solutions may help when they become bothersome.
When to talk to a professional
Hot flashes are very common during the transition to menopause. They’re linked in part to hormonal changes that affect how the brain regulates body temperature.

A small shift in body temperature can then feel like sudden heat. The body responds by dilating the blood vessels in the skin, which can cause a sensation of heat, flushing, and sometimes heavy sweating.
Some women experience a few episodes a week, while others may have several a day. Intensity and duration can also vary.
When they happen during sleep, hot flashes can cause night sweats. They can lead to repeated waking and make sleep less restful.

Lack of sleep can then increase fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and irritability during the day. It can therefore be helpful to factor sleep quality into how you assess the impact of your symptoms.
Breathable pajamas, light bedding, and a sufficiently cool bedroom can help limit discomfort at night.
Certain factors can trigger or intensify a hot flash. They don’t necessarily cause symptoms in everyone, but identifying them can help you better understand your own patterns.
An overheated room or clothing that’s too heavy
For a few weeks, note when your hot flashes happen, how intense they are, and what happened right before. This can help you spot your personal triggers.
Keep your space cool and well-ventilated
Practice slow breathing during a hot flash
These measures won’t necessarily make hot flashes disappear, but they can make episodes easier to manage and reduce discomfort when they occur.

Hot flashes are common during perimenopause and menopause. Still, you don’t have to simply put up with them if they become difficult to live with. A doctor or midwife can assess your symptoms and discuss the different options with you.
When should you make an appointment?
A consultation can be especially helpful when symptoms have a significant impact on your daily life or when you’d like to know what options are available.
Frequent hot flashes or night sweats that cause repeated waking, significant fatigue, or difficulty functioning normally during the day.
If hot flashes interfere with your work, activities, travel, social relationships, or simply your everyday comfort.
A clear increase in the frequency or intensity of symptoms is worth discussing in order to find the most suitable solutions.
Hormonal and non-hormonal options may be offered depending on your situation. A professional can help you weigh their benefits, risks, and any possible contraindications.

A hot flash can have different causes. Some symptoms may also be related to a medication, another medical condition, or a significant change in your health. If something feels unusual, new, or especially intense, it’s best to talk to a professional rather than automatically assuming it’s menopause.
Chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, feeling faint, sudden weakness, or unusual painful swelling in one leg require prompt medical attention.
Sudden shortness of breath or significant difficulty breathing
Sudden weakness, or trouble speaking or seeing
Painful, unusual swelling in one leg

If hot flashes are bothersome enough to need management, several approaches may be considered. Depending on your situation, the professional may discuss lifestyle measures, non-hormonal treatments, or, when appropriate, hormone therapy.
Treatment is chosen case by case
Age, symptoms, medical history, current treatments, and personal preferences can all influence the options offered.

Arriving with a bit of information can make the consultation more useful. You can track, for a few days or weeks, how often episodes occur, how intense they are, and their impact on your sleep or activities.
How often do your hot flashes happen?
How long have you been experiencing them?
Do they tend to happen during the day, at night, or both?
Do they disrupt your sleep or activities?
Are you currently taking any medication or hormonal contraception?
You don’t need to wait until symptoms become very severe before talking about them. A consultation can also simply help you understand what’s going on and learn about the solutions available.
Hot flashes are common during the menopause transition.
Identifying your triggers can help you manage episodes better.
Simple habits can reduce everyday discomfort.
If symptoms disrupt your sleep or daily life, talk to a professional.
Several management options may be discussed depending on your situation.

Hot flashes are common, but they shouldn’t be dismissed when they affect your sleep, work, or well-being. Paying attention to your symptoms and talking to a professional can help you better understand their cause and explore suitable solutions.
This article is for informational purposes only and doesn’t replace personalized medical advice.
Counterintuitive but true: staying well hydrated helps your body retain less water throughout your cycle.
Needs across the phases of your cycle
What to drink day to day
Counterintuitive but true: staying well hydrated helps the body retain less water and reduces bloating, especially toward the end of the cycle.
When the body is short on water, it tends to store more of it as a precaution. Drinking enough tells it, on the contrary, that it can release water more easily.
Your water needs stay fairly stable overall, with a few nuances depending on the phase:
A little extra water helps offset fluid loss and limit bloating.
Needs stay stable; a slight rise in body temperature can increase thirst.
Good hydration helps limit the feeling of puffiness often felt during this time.
Aim for about 1.5 to 2 liters a day, a little more during your period to offset fluid loss.
About 1.5 to 2 liters a day, a little more during your period.
Ginger or chamomile offer gentle hydration during cramps.
Limiting very sugary or caffeinated drinks can help toward the end of the cycle.
Fatigue with no other obvious explanation
A few simple habits are often enough to stay hydrated without even thinking about it:
Keep a water bottle within reach throughout the day
Pair a glass of water with a habit you already have (waking up, each meal)
Mix in herbal infusions if plain water gets dull
During physical activity, remember to drink before, during, and after exercise to make up for sweat loss.
"Drinking a lot makes me more bloated."
Good hydration helps the body retain less water.
Ginger or chamomile teas also offer soothing hydration during cramps.
Staying well hydrated helps the body retain less water and reduces bloating.
Aim for about 1.5 to 2 liters a day, a little more during your period.
Ginger or chamomile teas can also soothe during cramps.
Intense, persistent thirst is worth mentioning to a healthcare professional.
Informational content. This article does not replace personalized medical advice. If in doubt, seek guidance from a healthcare professional.

Distinguishing irregular bleeding from your usual period, with general markers to help guide you.
This content is purely educational. Religious questions should be validated by qualified scholars. AWA does not issue fatwas or personalized religious rulings.
Why can it be difficult to identify?
What to do in case of doubt?

Istihâda refers to bleeding that occurs outside the usual menstrual cycle, or that continues beyond the duration of menstruation recognized by Islamic tradition. Unlike menstruation (hayd) or nifas (bleeding after childbirth), it does not have the same ritual status: it is generally considered to be bleeding of a different nature, sometimes linked to a medical cause.
This content explains the concept in general terms; it does not allow you to determine whether a specific instance of bleeding corresponds to Istihâda in your personal situation.

It can be difficult to distinguish Istihâda from menstruation or an irregular cycle, because the bleeding can sometimes look similar, vary in intensity, or continue in an unusual way. This difficulty is recognized by scholars themselves, which explains why several approaches exist to identify it.
It is normal not to know right away what unusual bleeding corresponds to; this uncertainty is a common situation, not a mistake on your part.
Certain elements can help guide your thinking, without being universal rules, since the precise markers vary according to the schools of jurisprudence.
Duration compared to your usual cycle
Regularity or unusual nature of the bleeding
How the bleeding evolves over time
Possible presence of a known medical cause
These elements are general markers, not absolute criteria: they may be interpreted differently by scholars and schools of jurisprudence.
Taking the time to observe your bleeding over several days, without rushing, helps you better understand your own situation before drawing a conclusion.
Note the start date and, if possible, the usual length of your cycles
Observe whether the bleeding follows a pattern close to your previous periods
Do not rely on a single isolated day alone
Record these observations if you plan to consult a scholar or a healthcare professional

In the case of Istihâda, prayer and fasting generally remain obligatory, unlike during menstruation. Hygiene precautions (such as suitable protection) are then recommended to allow worship to continue, according to the methods taught by the different schools of jurisprudence.

The precise precautions (such as renewing ablutions) may vary depending on the school of jurisprudence followed; referring to the opinion you usually follow or to a qualified scholar helps you apply them correctly.
Persistent doubt about the nature of bleeding is a common situation, and should not be a source of excessive worry.
Refer to the usual duration and rhythm of your own periods
Consult a healthcare professional if the bleeding is unusual or prolonged
Ask a qualified scholar for their opinion on the religious dimension
Keep in mind that a general answer does not replace guidance suited to your situation

This content remains educational and general: it does not constitute a fatwa or an individual religious ruling. For any personal situation, especially in case of prolonged doubt, the opinion of a qualified scholar remains the reference.

Istihâda is a concept that distinguishes unusual bleeding from menstruation or nifas, with specific implications for prayer and fasting. In case of doubt, careful observation and the opinion of a qualified scholar remain the best resources.
How these strips work, and when to use them.
LH (luteinizing hormone) is produced by the brain and controls how the ovaries function. Ovulation tests detect the surge in this hormone, which triggers the release of the egg 24 to 36 hours later.
A urine test strip measures LH levels: a test line as dark as or darker than the control line indicates a surge.
It’s recommended to start testing a few days before the ovulation date estimated from your cycle.
Start a few days before the ovulation date estimated from the average length of your cycles.
Test at the same time each day
Ideally around midday, avoiding your first urine of the morning.
Limit large amounts of fluids in the hours before the test.
A positive result signals the most fertile time for intercourse over the following 1 to 2 days. A negative result simply means the surge hasn’t happened yet.
PCOS can cause naturally higher LH levels, which can blur the reading
Certain fertility treatments can affect the result
Very diluted urine can give a false negative
A lower-quality test can be less reliable
An LH surge indicates a triggering hormonal signal, but on its own it doesn’t guarantee that the egg was actually released.
Combining ovulation tests with your basal body temperature or cervical mucus observation gives a fuller picture of your cycle.
Ovulation tests detect the LH surge, which triggers the release of the egg 24 to 36 hours later.
It’s recommended to start testing a few days before the ovulation date estimated from your cycle.
